name: Tongkat Ali
summary: Tongkat ali is a South-East Asian shrub whose root extract is sold to raise testosterone, stress resilience and energy. Small trials show some benefits, but EFSA found in 2021 that its safety is not established.
commonUses: May ease stress and lift mood.
May raise energy and ease tiredness.
May help build muscle and improve body composition.
roles: It is a traditional herbal remedy. It is not an essential nutrient, and no needed role in the body is established.

status.note: This basic guide does not provide a routine status test.

high.note: See the cautions below; this guide does not establish a safe upper amount.

examples: Not eaten as a food; used as a root extract or powder

reference.noUpperLimit: No tolerable upper intake level has been set for tongkat ali. EFSA's 2021 opinion concluded that the safety of the extract it assessed was not established under any condition of use, so no safe amount can be stated. Absence of a limit is not proof that any amount is safe.

cautions: EFSA concluded in 2021 that the safety of a standardised Tongkat Ali water extract has not been established, because laboratory tests suggested it can damage DNA. Long-term safety in people is not known.
Human trials are small and short, several used one branded extract, and one reviewed study had no placebo group. Reviews call the evidence promising but limited.

People who are pregnant, breastfeeding, have a hormone-sensitive condition or take regular medicines should check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking a supplement. A supplement that changes hormones can also change lab results the app tracks. No specific drug interaction was verified here.

origin: Tongkat ali (Eurycoma longifolia Jack) is a shrub native to South-East Asia, where its root is used in traditional medicine and nicknamed "Malaysian ginseng". Its characteristic compounds include quassinoids such as eurycomanone, plus glycosaponins and alkaloids.

Supplements are usually a hot-water extract of the root, often a branded and standardised one, and the human trials mostly used such extracts. Most trials are small and short, and several tested one branded extract. In 2021 EFSA assessed a standardised water extract as a novel food for the EU and could not establish that it is safe.
dosage: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) assessed a standardised Tongkat Ali root water extract as a novel food in 2021, proposed for adults (not pregnant or breastfeeding women) at up to 200 mg a day. EFSA's panel found that the extract has the potential to damage DNA in laboratory tests, particularly in tissues of first contact such as the stomach and duodenum, and concluded that its safety had not been established under any condition of use. No tolerable upper intake level has been set.

An amount commonly used in studies and supplements is about 200 to 400 mg a day of a standardised water extract. Key trials used 200 mg a day for one month (men with symptoms of low testosterone), 200 mg a day for 6 months (together with training), 300 mg a day for 12 weeks (quality of life and sexual well-being) and 400 mg a day for 6 weeks (recreational athletes). This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

When reading a label, check that it is a root extract, the extract type (hot-water extract, alcohol extract or plain root powder), the standardisation (EFSA described glycosaponins 40 to 65 percent and eurycomanone 0.8 to 1.5 percent for the extract it assessed) and the amount of extract rather than raw root.

foodAmounts.verdict: Not applicable. Tongkat ali root is not eaten as an ordinary food; it is used as a root extract or powder, so there is no food amount to compare.
